To estimate the causal effect of higher household income on health outcomes, specifically the number of illness episodes, I will employ an instrumental variable (IV) approach. The treatment variable will be the log of household income per adult equivalent, while the outcome variable will be the number of illness episodes reported. The random assignment of village eligibility for the unconditional cash transfer serves as a credible instrument; it is expected that the cash transfer will increase household income without directly influencing health outcomes outside of the income channel. Key control variables will include age, sex, education, household size, distance to the nearest clinic, and rainfall deviations to account for potential confounding effects. The main threat to this design is that unobserved variables related to both income and health may still affect results, necessitating a robust check on the validity of the instrument and ensuring the exclusion restriction holds.

The key treatment variable will be the log of household income, while the outcome variable will be the number of reported illness episodes over the past four weeks. Village-level fixed effects will account for time-invariant heterogeneity, and individual fixed effects will control for time-varying unobservables. A potential main threat to identification is that other concurrent interventions or external factors might also influence health outcomes during the same period. To address this, I will include controls for seasonal rainfall deviations in my model, since they affect household income and could impact health outcomes as well. Furthermore, I will consider the share of clinic items and rainfall as control variables to minimize bias.

To estimate the causal effect of rural income growth on the number of Hindu-Muslim riots, I will employ a difference-in-differences (DiD) design, taking advantage of the 1985 random draw for the public-works program as a natural experiment. The treatment variable is the annual growth of district rural income per person, which I will measure using the ‘wage_firs_000’ and ‘crop_amou_107’ variables, and the outcome variable is the count of Hindu-Muslim riots per district-year. I will include district and year fixed effects to account for unobservable time-invariant characteristics and any common shocks affecting all districts within a given year. A key threat to this design is potential confounding from other economic or political factors that might differentially affect districts beyond the income treatment, such as local governance quality or prior historical tensions. Additionally, I will conduct robustness checks for parallel trends to validate my assumptions. I will also assess incentive compatibility of districts drawn for the program to ensure that the treatment effect is isolated from other contemporaneous changes.

To estimate the causal effect of schooling on log weekly wage, I will employ an instrumental variable (IV) approach, using quarter of birth (qob1) as an instrument for completed years of schooling. This approach leverages the observation that men born in early months may complete fewer years of school due to school-entry rules, allowing for traction in causal inference despite non-random assignment of education levels. The key variables in this analysis will include the treatment variable (years of completed schooling) and the outcome variable (log weekly wage in 1979), while controlling for variables such as race (black), marital status (married), Metropolitan Statistical Area (smsa), region, age, and the responses to socioeconomic indicators. The primary threat to identification is the potential for the quarter of birth variable to be correlated with unobserved characteristics that also affect earnings, such as family background or early-life investments in education. However, the strong theoretical justification for the quarter of birth as an exogenous source of variation mitigates this risk considerably.
